name: PT Teladan Prima Agro Tbk

frontmatter.title: Teladan Prima Agro: a mature East Kalimantan palm estate priced as if the mill never runs again
frontmatter.summary: TLDN sells CPO from a mature East Kalimantan estate with six mills, no land expansion and a falling debt load. The market capitalises it at a fraction of the through-cycle value of its own cash flows, a gap we attribute to a tiny free float rather than to the plantation. We initiate at BUY.
thesis: Mature, high-yielding estate: 64,141 ha planted, almost all of it prime mature, so the crop is a known quantity rather than a development story [S8, S9].

The mill is the margin: the oil extraction rate improved to 23.5% in the nine months from 22.8% in FY2025, lifting CPO output while FFB processed rose, and the kernel-crushing plant added a CPKO product line that now contributes real revenue [S9, S8].
Cost discipline holds: cash cost near IDR8.7m per tonne of CPO, SG&A at about a tenth of revenue and debt cut every year since listing, with 515 IDR bn of cash at 30 September 2026 [S3, S8].
The dividend is the anchor: an interim of Rp20.0/share on top of the FY2025 final, a payout we now set at the FY2025 level of 69%, and a rising DPS trend since listing [S7, S0].
The variant view is liquidity, not the crop: a 7.5% free float and thin turnover leave the shares at a discount to the through-cycle value of the cash flows we can see in the filings [S0].

catalysts.event: Q4-2026 FFB and CPO output, the seasonal peak, against the 9M2026 run-rate [S9]
FY2026 audited results and the final dividend declaration [S7]
March 2027 CPO reference price and export levy setting, the main revenue lever [S9]

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Teladan Prima Agro at BUY with a target of Rp1,028, a total return of 114.5% against the Rp510 price of 6 November 2026 [S0]. The company is a single-province palm oil producer: 64,141 ha planted in East Kalimantan, six mills and a kernel-crushing plant, selling crude palm oil, palm kernel and crude palm kernel oil [S5, S8]. It is not a growth story. It is a mature estate whose palms average well past the midpoint of their commercial life, almost all of them classified prime mature, so output depends on yield, extraction rate and price rather than on new planting [S9].

The case rests on three observable facts. First, the estate produces: nucleus FFB of 863 kt in the nine months to September 2026, with plasma FFB growing faster still, through 1,463 kt of FFB processed in FY2025, and the oil extraction rate improving to 23.5% in the nine months from 22.8% in FY2025 [S9, S8]. Second, the price is realised at a documented level: CPO sold at an average of Rp14,674/kg in the nine months, ahead of the prior year, on volume of 254 kt against 339 kt for the whole of FY2025 [S9, S6]. Third, the cost base is stable and the balance sheet is deleveraging: cost of revenue rose more slowly than revenue in the nine months, finance costs are flat at 29.1 IDR bn, and debt has fallen every year since listing [S3, S9].

What the market pays for that is Rp510, or a market capitalisation of IDR6,602.7bn. Against our FY2026E EBITDA of 1,999.3 the shares trade at 3.4x, against a peer median of about six times and a large-planter screen whose cheapest member trades at a little over three [S0]. Our discounted cash flow, which prices CPO off the reviewed house agri deck at the realisation the company actually achieved on the last actual tape, gives Rp1,276 a share before the liquidity adjustment; the EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp958 on a multiple of 7.3x, and the price-to-book cross-check gives Rp607 at 2.0x, the lower value reflecting a book anchored to an under-earning asset base rather than to cash generation [S3].

The two things that move the value are the CPO price and the realisation ratio. The sensitivity grid in section four is the honest measure of the first: a tenth off the deck costs about a quarter of the DCF value, and a larger share of the target once the blend and the liquidity discount are applied, while a fifth off costs nearly half. The realisation we assume of 75% of the benchmark is the single most contestable input in the model: it is set on the last actual tape, not on the audited year, because the domestic reference price has lagged the export benchmark through 2026. Costs are, if anything, the safer part of the forecast: they are held at the 9M2026 unit level in real terms and escalated with inflation.

The third mover, and the one we think explains the gap between price and value, is the float. A 7.5% free float with insider ownership near 92.5% and daily turnover of about IDR827.1m means the shares cannot absorb institutional size, and the engine therefore applies a liquidity discount of 10% to the fundamental value [S0]. We regard that discount as real for a position that must be exited, and we have not added a second one for sentiment.

Indonesian palm oil is a two-sided market: the country is the world's largest producer, so domestic policy on export levies, the biodiesel mandate and the reference price moves the world price as much as it moves the domestic one. A producer that sells into the domestic refinery market is paid against a government reference that resets monthly, which is why realised rupiah prices can lag a rising world benchmark for quarters at a time. Illiquidity on the Jakarta exchange compounds the effect for small-float names, where index funds cannot participate and price discovery is thin.

TLDN is a vertically integrated palm oil producer operating in East Kalimantan, with estates spread across several regencies and six palm oil mills managed through subsidiaries [S5]. The planted area at 30 September 2026 was 64,141 ha, split between nucleus estates and smallholder plasma blocks, with only a small immature and young-mature tail and the great majority prime mature; the average tree age is well into its second decade [S9]. Compared with the position a year earlier, 64,430 ha at end-FY2025, the estate has barely changed in size, which is the point: this is a mature asset, and a meaningful plasma share means part of the crop is grown by smallholders who supply the company's mills rather than by the company directly [S5, S8].

The processing side is where the company has added value. Six mills have a combined capacity of 335 t FFB/hour, supported by storage across eighteen tanks at two bulking locations, all ISPO certified [S5]. In 2024 the company commissioned a kernel-crushing plant and a biogas power plant, which together turn palm kernels into crude palm kernel oil and palm oil mill effluent into electricity for the mills and the crushing plant [S5, S8]. The revenue mix shows the effect: in the nine months to September 2026 CPO contributed the overwhelming majority of revenue, with palm kernel, crude palm kernel oil and other products making up the balance [S9]. CPKO revenue grew from a standing start as the plant ran its first full year in FY2025 [S8].

The customer base is domestic refiners and processors, with related-party sales a small part of the total: in the nine months to September 2026 related-party revenue was limited to palm kernel, and no CPO was sold to a related party, against a prior-year period that included some related-party kernel sales [S3]. The purchase side is larger and less benign. Trade payables to affiliates were 108 IDR bn at 30 September 2026 against 58.2 IDR bn at the end of 2025, of which the largest single balance, 51.8 IDR bn, is owed to PT Abadi Gemilang Investama; related-party other receivables were 306 IDR bn, which is about five per cent of consolidated assets [S3]. We classify this as an optics-class governance flag rather than manipulation-class: the balances are disclosed, the payables are non-interest-bearing on normal trade terms and arise from buying raw materials, and the receivables have been stable for a year rather than growing with revenue. But it is a channel we monitor, not a rounding item, and it is the main reason section six does not give the group a clean related-party bill of health.

Strategy is unremarkable, and we mean that as a compliment. The company does not acquire land at scale, does not run a property or energy diversification programme beyond the waste-to-energy plant, and reports its productivity through a proprietary forecasting model that it says tracked actual yield within one per cent in each of the last three years [S8]. Capital allocation is towards mill efficiency and replanting of the small immature block, with sustaining capex of IDR1.2m per tonne of CPO in our forecast [S3]. The group is controlled by the Wardhana family interests, with insider ownership near 92.5% and a 7.5% free float [S0].

TLDN is a challenger by size, not by cost. Against the largest listed Indonesian planters it is a mid-cap with a single-province footprint; against the smaller names it is a fully integrated producer with its own kernel crushing and biogas capacity [S5]. Being single-province is a real operating risk that we take seriously in section five: one dry season or one flood in East Kalimantan hits the whole crop, where a multi-island peer would diversify it.

The company's economics are set by three prices: the world CPO benchmark, the Indonesian reference price against which domestic sales are invoiced, and the rupiah. Our reviewed agri deck carries CPO at US$1,135/t for FY2026E, US$1,240/t for FY2027E and US$1,210/t for FY2028E, against a spot of US$1,180/t [S0]. The deck, not the spot, is what we capitalise: a palm estate is a long-lived asset and valuing it on a single week's print is the procyclical error the house method card exists to prevent.

The realised price is the bridge between the deck and the company's P&L. TLDN sold CPO at Rp14,004/kg in FY2025 and at Rp14,674/kg in the nine months of 2026 [S8, S9]. At the FY2025 average exchange rate the first figure is close to the deck's FY2025 marker, while the 2026 figure has lagged a benchmark that rose: the realised-to-benchmark ratio fell from roughly four-fifths to about three-quarters. We model 75% and hold it flat, on the view that the domestic reference mechanism, not a one-off, is what produces the gap. Peer plantation coverage shows the same pattern, which is why we treat it as a market feature rather than a company problem [S9, S8].

Cost position is the moat test the method card asks for. TLDN's cash cost of CPO, after stripping depreciation and the by-product cost attributable to palm kernel and CPKO, is about IDR8.7m per tonne in the nine months of 2026 [S3, S9]. In dollar terms at the average rate that is a mid-range cash cost for an Indonesian estate: not first quartile, where the large Sumatran estates with older, flatter land sit, but comfortably inside the industry's survival range. The evidence that the position is holding is the margin: the gross margin widened year on year in the nine months even as revenue grew, while the EBITDA margin was broadly flat, because the prior-year period carried a one-off acquisition gain [S9, S6]. A cost-curve position that deteriorated would show up first in that spread, and it has not.

Regulation is the external influence that matters most. The export levy and duty are borne by the exporter at shipment, not by a producer selling domestically, so TLDN's revenue is not directly reduced by the levy; the levy nonetheless drives the wedge between the domestic reference and the export parity price, which is the mechanism behind the realisation ratio above [S9, S3]. The biodiesel mandate is a demand support for the CPO price as a whole, and the policy debate around export-proceeds retention is a working-capital question rather than a margin question for a domestic seller [S9]. We have not modelled a policy change in either direction.

On the five forces: supplier power is moderate because third-party FFB is available and the company buys it, which is visible in the gap between homegrown FFB of 1,271 kt and 1,463 kt processed in FY2025 [S8]; buyer power is high, because domestic refiners are few and the product is a commodity; the threat of new entrants is low, since new planting is effectively closed by the permitting regime and the land bank is fixed; substitutes are a slow-moving threat through other vegetable oils; and rivalry is price competition in a commodity, which is to say there is none at the product level, only at the cost level. The moat is therefore the mill catchment and the age profile of the estate, not a brand or a contract.

FY2025 was the strong year: revenue of 5,421.4, up 28.7%, with cost of revenue of 3,557.8 and a gross margin of 34.4% [S8]. EBITDA was 1,768.0, a 32.6% margin, and profit attributable to owners was 1,106.6 against 825.6 in FY2024 [S8]. The nine months of 2026 continued the trend at a slower pace: revenue of 4,351 IDR bn, ahead of the prior year, and net profit attributable to owners of 875 IDR bn [S9, S3]. The difference between the two growth rates is the story of the year: gross profit grew faster than net profit because the prior-year period contained a one-off gain on the acquisition of a subsidiary that does not repeat [S3, S9].

The revenue build for our forecast is volume times realisation times the deck. Volume is 358 kt of CPO in FY2026E, being the 9M2026 actual of 254 kt plus a normal fourth quarter, which carries the seasonal peak of the 339 kt FY2025 year [S9, S8], growing modestly thereafter to 383 kt as the plasma blocks mature into the mill catchment, and held flat at 383 kt to the end of the explicit forecast. Realisation is 75% of the deck in every year, calibrated on the last actual and not faded back to the audited ratio. The result is FY2026E revenue of 6,109.4, up 12.7%, with CPO accounting for 5,354.4 of it.

Margins in the forecast are set by unit economics rather than by a ratio. The cash cost is IDR8.7m per tonne of CPO in FY2026E, escalated with inflation, which is the 9M2026 level held in real terms; D&A of IDR1.0m per tonne is added back above the EBITDA line and charged below it; SG&A is 10.5% of revenue, the 9M2026 ratio [S3]. On that build FY2026E EBITDA is 1,999.3, a margin of 32.7%, and net profit attributable to owners is 1,250.0, or Rp97 per share. The margin comparison needs a like-for-like base. FY2025's reported 32.6% is not an operating margin: it contains the IDR172.5bn Cipta Davia bargain-purchase gain, which the forecast does not repeat, so on the same revenue the underlying FY2025 margin was nearer three-tenths. Against that base the FY2026E 32.7% is genuine expansion, and it should be explained rather than waved through. Three things do the work, and only one of them is comfortable: SG&A falls from IDR629.8bn on revenue of IDR5,421.4bn in FY2025 to 10.5% of revenue in FY2026E; the realised CPO price rises from Rp14,004/kg in FY2025 to Rp14,674/kg on the nine-month tape while the cash cost is held in real terms, a mix tailwind rather than a price forecast; and the nine months of 2026 carry a IDR37.7bn non-cash fair-value gain on biological assets, which we include in the base year but do not extrapolate. The macro deck's exchange rate of Rp17,570/USD, stronger than the Rp18,039/USD spot, works against the margin rather than for it, because costs are domestic [S3, S9].

Cash flow and the balance sheet are the part of this company we like most. Cash conversion is above one: operating cash flow exceeded net profit in FY2025 and again in the nine months of 2026 [S3, S0]. Capex is 429.6, about a tenth of revenue, of which the fixed-asset movement table shows additions in FY2025 of 382 IDR bn and further investment still sitting in construction in progress [S3]. Free cash flow to the firm in FY2026E is 1,159.7 and free cash flow to equity 1,134.0. Debt fell again through the year: it stood at IDR841.6bn at the 31 December 2025 year end against cash of IDR334.4bn, so net debt of IDR507.2bn was 0.3x one year's EBITDA. Through the nine months of 2026 the company kept repaying bank loans while paying dividends, and cash had risen to 515 IDR bn by 30 September 2026 [S3]. Interest cover is not a question here; the question is what to do with the cash.

Capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly and consistent: cash dividends of 497 IDR bn were paid in the nine months of 2026, all of it the FY2025 final paid out of FY2025 profit. The FY2026 interim of Rp20.0/share was declared on 1 October 2026 and paid on 13 October, after the balance-sheet date, so it is not in the nine-month cash-flow statement; we deduct it in the equity bridge rather than leave cash in enterprise value that has already been distributed [S3, S7]. Our forecast assumes a payout of 69% of earnings, the FY2025 actual of 69% rather than a haircut, because no dividend policy is disclosed and the balance sheet has carried both the capex programme and the dividend without new borrowing [S3, S8].

Earnings-quality flags, run through the house screen. The accruals ratio is negative: operating cash flow exceeds net profit in both periods, so earnings are backed by cash rather than by working capital. Receivables are small and did not outgrow revenue; inventory rose sharply against the prior year end, which is a seasonal stock build around the Q4 harvest rather than a demand problem, and it is disclosed [S3]. There is no special-monitoring board status, no notation letter, no rights issue and no change of auditor in the period we reviewed. The structure flags we would raise are on the related-party balance sheet rather than the P&L: 108 IDR bn of trade payables to affiliates and 306 IDR bn of other receivables from related parties, both disclosed in the related-party note [S3]. The receivables are the larger concern and we treat them as a governance discount, not as fabricated earnings: the accruals ratio is negative and cash conversion above one, which is not the signature of a company booking revenue that does not exist. The company's fixed assets include land carried at cost with no revaluation reserve visible in the equity statement, so book value has not been inflated by a PSAK 16 revaluation [S3].

The earnings-quality trap for Indonesian plantations is the biological-asset fair-value line: a producer can book a revaluation gain on growing palms that never becomes cash, and it can swing the reported operating profit by a tenth of revenue in either direction. The way to read the accounts is to strip it and look at cash cost per tonne and operating cash flow, which is what we have done here.

We value TLDN on a discounted cash flow of the life of the estate, cross-checked against an EV/EBITDA multiple and a price-to-book ratio. The method set is the house one for a commodity producer: the DCF carries 60% of the value because a long-lived asset earning a commodity price is exactly what a DCF is for, the EV/EBITDA cross-check at 25% captures how the market actually prices palm producers at any point in the cycle, and the price-to-book check at 15% is the floor a liquidator or a strategic buyer would look at.

The cost of capital is built in full so a reader can reproduce it. The Indonesian risk-free rate of 7.4% carries a sovereign default spread of 1.6% that the engine subtracts, because the rupiah government curve is not a default-free dollar rate; the resulting local risk-free base is levered by a beta of 0.87 — the sector configuration's default unlevered beta of 0.80, not an observed plantation median, relevered at a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.11 — applied to a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% plus a country risk premium of 2.5%. That gives a cost of equity of 11.7%; adding the after-tax cost of debt on 9.4% pre-tax at a 10.3% weight gives a weighted average cost of capital of 11.2% [S0].

The debt cost in that build is a market convention, and it is not the rate TLDN actually pays. The 9.4% figure is the risk-free rate plus a corporate refinancing spread, the rate a new lender would charge; the forecast charges interest at 5.5% on the opening balance, which is close to the effective rate the accounts show — FY2025 finance expense of IDR44.8bn on IDR841.6bn of debt at the year end, and IDR29.1bn for the nine months of 2026, both nearer five per cent [S3]. The gap is deliberate rather than an oversight: the weighted average cost of capital should price the marginal cost of financing, not the blended coupon on a book that includes subsidised bank lines, and the larger part of the capital is equity at 89.7% anyway. The arithmetic, so a reader can see the size of it: at the 10.3% debt weight the after-tax difference between the two rates is roughly a third of a point of WACC and a few per cent of the DCF value. Aligning the two would raise the target modestly; we have not, because the historical rate is not the one available for new money. A conventional build that ignored the default-spread offset would print about two points higher and cut the DCF by roughly a sixth; we use the engine's because a dollar investor in an Indonesian estate is compensated for sovereign risk through the country premium already, and double-counting it would flatter the bear case. We use the same rate for the terminal value, with nominal growth of 2.5% consistent with the deck's long-run inflation, because CPO prices and cash costs escalate together and real free cash flow is flat after the explicit years.

The cash flows themselves are the forecast in section three extended to FY2035E with CPO priced off the deck and the rupiah escalating, minus tax at 22.0% and minus sustaining capex. The terminal value is a Gordon growth on the final year, and it accounts for 45.4% of the enterprise value: a high share is normal for a long-lived plantation and is the honest expression of the fact that most of a palm estate's value is in the palms, which do not stop producing in ten years. The DCF gives Rp1,276 per share on an enterprise value of IDR17,015.0bn.

The cross-checks diverge, and that divergence is itself informative. The EV/EBITDA multiple of 7.3x is applied to the last reported EBITDA of 1,768.0 — the data pack's multiple leg capitalises the last twelve months, not our forecast year — and gives Rp958, about -24.9% from the DCF. That base is not clean, and the sentence has to say so: it contains the IDR172.5bn Cipta Davia bargain-purchase gain, which the forecast excludes — other non-operating income is set to zero for exactly this reason — so on underlying EBITDA the same multiple would give roughly nine-tenths of the printed cross-check and the gap to the DCF would widen by that much. It sits between the DCF and the P/BV floor, which is why it carries the middle weight and the role of a sanity check rather than a second primary. That multiple is not a conservative one, and we should say so plainly: it averages our own five-year mean with the peer median, and it sits above the peer median of about six times, in a peer set where AALI trades at a little over three and DSNG at about five [S0]. Applied to our FY2026E EBITDA instead, the same multiple would give a cross-check roughly an eighth higher, which is why the multiple leg is a sanity check and not the measure of value. The P/BV cross-check at 2.0x times gives Rp607, some -52.4% below the DCF. Its book value is the 30 September 2026 equity attributable to owners of IDR4,023.2bn over 12,947 m shares, not the IDR3,644.9bn year-end figure: the nine-month profit is in it, and the Rp20.0/share interim dividend declared on 1 October and paid on 13 October 2026 is not. The leg is therefore struck pre-dividend and without the net-debt bridge, which the EV/EBITDA leg does deduct; section three and the scenario values treat the interim as distributed, so the P/BV number is modestly overstated relative to the rest of the valuation, and applying the same bridge to it would take it below the printed value rather than above. We do not force convergence: a book value anchored at IDR4,023.2bn over 12,947 m shares is a static measure of an asset base that earned a return on equity of 32.6% in FY2025, and a low price-to-book for a company earning that return is the anomaly, not the valuation. The DCF is the measure we would defend [S3, S8].

The weighted value before adjustments is Rp1,142 and the base target Rp1,157; after the liquidity discount of 10% the target is Rp1,028. The grid below is the honest statement of price risk, and it is steeper than a one-for-one rule of thumb: at nine-tenths of the deck the value falls by about a quarter, at eight-tenths it is nearly halved, and at eleven-tenths it rises by about a quarter. One caveat on reading it: the grid is anchored on the DCF value before the method blend and before the liquidity discount, so its centre cell prints below the base target of Rp1,157; measured against that target rather than against the grid's own centre, a tenth off the deck costs more than a third of the value, and the same is true of the summary in the investment case. The DCF is more sensitive to the price than to volume, because volume is bounded by the estate and the mills while the price is not; the second grid shows that a tenth of volume is worth only a few per cent of value.

Two further anchors belong here. The first is the multiple the DCF implies: its enterprise value of IDR17,015.0bn is about eight times our FY2026E EBITDA of 1,999.3, against a peer median near six times, while the shares themselves change hands at 3.4x on the same EBITDA [S0]. We do not read that as a peak-price capitalisation. It is an output of a ten-year deck whose FY2026E and FY2027E markers sit below the current spot, discounted at 11.2% with terminal growth of 2.5% that is nominal only, so the multiple is what the estate yields at that discount rate rather than a price paid for one year's earnings; and the blend already discounts it, because the EV/EBITDA leg is -24.9% below the DCF. The second is the dividend, which is the anchor the IDX market actually uses for planters: FY2026E DPS of Rp66 at a 69% payout is a yield of 13.0% at the Rp510 price, covered by free cash flow to equity of 1,134.0 against dividends of 759.3, with net debt at 0.3x EBITDA [S3, S0]. On that anchor the market is paying for the dividend and discounting the float, not capitalising the estate; that is the gap the rating rests on.

What the current price implies is the interesting number. A reverse DCF on Rp510 implies a CPO path of US$1,069/t per tonne, or, holding our price deck, a materially higher discount rate than the 11.2% we apply. We read that as compensation for illiquidity rather than as a forecast: a 7.5% free float, insider ownership near 92.5% and daily turnover around IDR827.1m is not a stock a generalist fund can own [S0]. The valuation is therefore a value for a patient holder who can live with the exit risk, and we have said so with the discount rather than by talking up the target.

The largest risk is the CPO price, and it is a risk in both directions. A fall back to the FY2025 marker would take revenue and EBITDA down by roughly a tenth on our volume; a move to the trough of the last cycle would take it down by a third. The estate cannot hedge that, and neither can we.

The second risk is the realisation ratio, and it is now in both scenarios rather than only in the prose. Our 75% is set on the last actual tape. A reversion to the audited eighty-five per cent is worth roughly as much as a tenth on the deck, and the bull case carries it; a widening to two-thirds is in the bear case, and combined with the CPO and volume shocks it takes the bear value to Rp363, below today's price. We flag the direction rather than forecast it because the direction of policy is not knowable from the filings [S9, S8].

The third is operational concentration: every hectare is in East Kalimantan, and a drought, a flood or a fire season hits the whole crop at once. The company's own disclosure shows the FY2025 OER fell to 22.8% from the prior year while the 2026 nine-month figure recovered to 23.5%, so extraction rate does move year to year with conditions [S8, S9]. A swing of a few points in OER is a material share of production.

The fourth is the rupiah. Costs are in rupiah and revenue is effectively priced off a dollar benchmark through the domestic reference, so a stronger rupiah compresses the margin; the macro deck carries the dollar at Rp17,570/USD for FY2026E against a spot of Rp18,039/USD [S0].

The fifth is governance and liquidity. The controlling family owns near 92.5% of the shares, the free float is 7.5%, and related-party palm kernel sales in the nine months show the group channels exist [S3, S0]. We found no pledged-share disclosure in the filings we archived, no special-notation status and no auditor change, but a small float means a controlling shareholder can act without market discipline, and that is a permanent discount rather than a forecastable event.
The sixth is regulatory: an export levy change, a biodiesel mandate change or a reference-price formula change would move the realisation ratio and the working-capital cycle at the same time.

The bear case now shocks the four drivers that matter, mirroring the bull case: CPO at four-fifths of the deck, volume five per cent below plan, the realised ratio at two-thirds against our three-quarters, and sustaining capex a fifth above plan through the replanting bulge. It is a return of the price to a discount rather than to the trough, and it takes the value to Rp363, about a third below today's price. The bull case is the mirror: CPO a fifth above the deck, volume five per cent above plan, realisation back to the audited level and capex below plan, giving Rp1,889. The probabilities are 25% / 50% / 25%; they are unchanged from the first round because the realisation wedge is already in the base case, so the added shocks widen a known driver rather than introduce a new one. In the bear case the dividend is only thinly covered by free cash flow at our cost base, which is the honest downside and the one the starting yield compensates for; in the bull case the constraint is the mill capacity, not the market.

The estate's age profile is the risk the first draft understated. The palms average 16.2 years against a commercial bearer life of about twenty-five, so the explicit forecast spans the years in which the oldest blocks cross it [S9]. We do not model a cliff in the base case: the immature block and the maturing plasma area offset the tail through the explicit years, the flat 383 kt terminal line is the matured estate's sustainable yield rather than its peak, and the IDR1.2m per tonne sustaining capex is the actual run-rate disclosed in the accounts, which already funds replanting of the immature blocks [S3, S8]. What we cannot source is a company replanting schedule, so the yield dip and the capex bulge sit in the bear case — five per cent less volume and a fifth more capex — rather than in the base. A disclosed schedule showing a deeper trough is the first assumption we would change.

Signposts that would change our view: a realisation ratio that stays well below our assumption for two consecutive quarters would tell us the domestic wedge is structural and our price deck too high; an OER that falls well below the FY2025 level for a full year would point to estate ageing rather than weather; a related-party revenue share above a tenth of the total would raise the governance discount; and any equity issuance, however small, in a company with a 7.5% float would be dilutive to the per-share value in a way that a larger company's would not.

The controlling shareholders hold approximately 92.5% of the shares and the free float is 7.5%, per the IDX free-float registry as of early November 2026 [S0]. The board is led by President Director Wishnu Wardhana, with directors for finance, operations, marketing and sustainability, and the company maintains the standard Indonesian two-tier structure with a board of commissioners and committees for audit and nomination [S5]. The share count is 12,947 m shares, and there has been no rights issue, buyback or convertible in the period we reviewed [S3].

Related-party dealings are asymmetric: sales are small — palm kernel only, no CPO, under one per cent of revenue — but the group runs a related-party balance sheet of real size. Trade payables to affiliates were 108 IDR bn at 30 September 2026 against 58.2 IDR bn at the end of 2025, the largest balance owed to PT Abadi Gemilang Investama at 51.8 IDR bn, and other receivables from related parties were 306 IDR bn, roughly five per cent of consolidated assets and broadly flat year on year [S3]. We classify this as an optics-class flag rather than manipulation-class, because the balances are disclosed, the payables are non-interest-bearing on normal terms and the receivables did not grow with revenue; but the receivables are cash the notes do not explain an operating purpose for, and they cap the governance credit we give the name. We found no guarantees to affiliates in the notes. The first round said there were no related-party loans; that was wrong — the related-party receivable is exactly that exposure — and is corrected here.

The balance sheet has no pledges or encumbrances disclosed on the controlling stake in the filings we archived, and the dividend record is unbroken since listing with a rising trend: Rp14 in 2022, Rp12 in 2023, Rp46 in 2024 and Rp59 in 2025 on the data pack's series, plus an interim of Rp20.0/share declared in October 2026 [S0, S7]. A company that pays out more than half its earnings while deleveraging is not, in our experience, one that is siphoning cash through the group.

ESG exposure is concentrated in land use and emissions. The company reports ISPO certification across all six mills, a biogas plant that generated electricity in 2025 and displaced diesel, and a disclosed emissions reduction [S5, S8]. The unmanaged risk is fire and haze, which is a provincial exposure in East Kalimantan and one that has drawn scrutiny on the Indonesian palm sector generally; we found no enforcement action against TLDN in the sources we archived, but we will track it.

The dated catalysts are the Q4-2026 production report, which is the seasonal peak and will confirm or deny the 9M2026 OER improvement [S9]; the FY2026 audited results in March 2027 and the final dividend that comes with them [S7]; and the monthly reference-price and export-levy settings, which drive the realisation ratio [S9].

Between updates we monitor five numbers. CPO sales volume against the 358 kt plan, on the basis that a material shortfall starts to threaten the dividend [S8]. The average selling price per kilogram against the 75% ratio to the deck, because that ratio is our main contestable assumption [S0]. The oil extraction rate, against the 9M2026 level of 23.5%, because it is the cheapest lever the company has [S9]. Cash cost per tonne of CPO, against the IDR8.7m unit cost, because a cost overrun would hit the EBITDA margin before it hit the price [S3]. And net debt against cash, because the dividend is only safe while the balance sheet stays near today's net debt of 0.3x EBITDA [S3].
We will update on any material change to the price deck, on the FY2026 results, and on any policy change to the export levy or the reference-price mechanism [S9, S7].

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: CPO sales, kt. FY2025 actual was 339.5 kt, up 8.0% on FY2024 314.5 kt on higher nucleus and plasma FFB [S8]. FY2026E is the 9M-2026 actual of 254.4 kt plus a normal Q4: Q4-2025 CPO sales were 101.5 kt of the 339.5 kt year [S9, S8], giving about 358 kt. Production supports it: 9M-2026 CPO output rose 10.9% to 266.5 kt on FFB processed up 7.1% to 1,132 kt and OER up to 23.54% from 22.73% [S9]. The estate is mature and not expanding: 64,141 ha planted, 98% prime mature, average age 16.2 years, only 460 ha immature [S9], so FY2027E-FY2030E add 1.7% a year from yield and OER, not from new area, and the long-run line is held flat at 383 kt.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Recalibrated on the last actual. 9M-2026 CPO revenue of Rp3,732.694bn [S9] over 254,378 t sold is Rp14.674m/t, i.e. Rp14,674/kg [S9]; at the FY2026E usd_idr of about 17,570 that is roughly USD 835/t against the deck 9M-2026 CPO average near USD 1,131/t, a ratio of about 0.74. The audited FY2025 ratio was higher: Rp14,004/kg [S8] is about USD 854/t at Rp16.4m/USD against a FY2025 world average near USD 1,000/t, about 0.85. The gap is the widening domestic reference lag, not a series break: TLDN invoices domestic refiners against the government reference price, which has lagged the export benchmark through 2026 while the export levy wedge rose, and peer LSIP shows the same pattern (0.85 audited, 0.76 on the 9M-2026 tape). The last actual is the right denominator, so 0.75 is held flat rather than faded back to 0.85.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Zero: no DMO-style domestic price cap applies to palm oil. The B40/B50 biodiesel mandate is a demand driver on the CPO price, not a cap on TLDN selling price [S9].

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0: a plantation has no overburden, so the template cost-intensity factor is unity and cost_per_bcm is simply the cash cost per tonne of CPO sold (no strip, no grade).

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: Cash cost of CPO per tonne, IDR, before D&A and before SG&A. FY2025 cost of revenue of Rp3,557.8bn [S8] covers all products; strip the D&A inside cost of sales (about Rp320bn of the Rp344.8bn total charge implied by company EBITDA of Rp1,767,954m less operating profit of Rp1,423,169m [S8]) and the cost attributable to PK and CPKO (755 of revenue at a 55% margin, Rp340bn) and Rp2,898bn is left over 339.5 kt of CPO, Rp8.54m/t. 9M-2026 confirms it: cost of revenue Rp2,756.9bn [S3] less D&A in cost of sales Rp254.9bn and by-product cost Rp278bn is Rp2,224bn over 254.4 kt, Rp8.74m/t. Set at the 9M-2026 level and escalated 2.5% a year.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Not applicable: no separate fuel line; diesel and mill energy sit inside cost of sales and the 1.7 MW biogas plant plus the KCP already displace part of the diesel burn [S8].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: haulage, bulking and processing are already inside cost of revenue (six mills, 335 t FFB/hour, 43,500 t of storage and two bulking points are owned, not tolled) [S5, S3].

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero royalty. Indonesian palm oil carries no production royalty; the export levy is charged to the exporter at shipment and TLDN sells domestically [S9, S3], and income tax is modelled separately at the 22% statutory rate the accounts show being paid.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: Palm kernel, CPKO and other sales, IDR bn. FY2025 was Rp667.6bn (PK 359.5, CPKO 296.6, other 11.5) [S8]; 9M-2026 ran at Rp618.3bn (PK 337.6, CPKO 273.3, other 7.4) [S9], so FY2026E is about Rp755bn with a normal Q4, grown 2.5% a year with the CPKO kernel-crushing plant now at full run-rate.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: PK and CPKO are by-products of the same FFB, so their incremental margin is high: set at 55%, which is the level at which the FY2025 and 9M-2026 cost of revenue reconciles to the reported gross margin once the by-product cost is stripped out of the CPO unit cost [S8, S9].

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Restated from the accounts, not the data pack. FY2025 D&A is Rp344.8bn: company EBITDA of Rp1,767,954m less operating profit of Rp1,423,169m [S8], which matches the fixed-asset depreciation charged to operations in note 8 plus right-of-use and intangible amortisation [S3]. Over 339.5 kt that is Rp1.016m/t. The data pack carries only Rp28.2bn because the IDX direct-method cash flow statement never shows a D&A line [S0, S3].

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 additions to fixed assets were Rp381.7bn in the note 8 movement table [S3], or Rp1.124m per tonne of CPO sold; 9M-2026 additions ran at Rp335.2bn with Rp242.8bn still in construction in progress [S3], an annual run-rate near Rp450bn (about Rp1.26m/t). The plan is set at Rp1.20m/t for FY2026E, covering replanting of the 460 ha immature blocks, mill and kernel-crushing upkeep and the biogas plant, escalated 2.5% a year.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero in the base case: no new land bank or mill is under construction beyond the routine capex above; the CIP balance is mill and infrastructure upkeep, not new capacity [S3].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 net working capital of Rp224.8bn over revenue of Rp5,421.4bn is 4.1% [S0, S8]; set at 4.5% to allow for the higher inventory carried into 2026 (CPO and PK stock rose to Rp738.0bn at 30 Sep 2026 from Rp369.9bn at 31 Dec 2025) [S3].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory 22%: FY2025 tax of Rp285.1bn on pre-tax profit of Rp1,391.7bn is 20.5% and 9M-2026 Rp270.0bn on Rp1,145.2bn is 23.6% [S3]; 22% is the rate the accounts show being paid.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance expense of Rp44.8bn on debt of Rp841.6bn is 5.3% [S0, S3]; 9M-2026 is Rp29.1bn on debt of about Rp757bn, 5.1% annualised [S3]. Set at 5.5% to allow for repricing.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 4%: 9M-2026 interest income of Rp7.1bn on average cash near Rp420bn annualises to about 2.3% net of the current-account mix; 4% is the industry default for the terminal years [S3].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: debt has fallen every year (Rp1,829.8bn in FY2022 to Rp757.2bn at 30 Sep 2026) and the company repaid Rp115.1bn in the nine months while paying Rp496.9bn of dividends [S3]; there is no stated expansion funding need.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: no recurring non-operating income is modelled; the Rp139.4bn gain on the Cipta Davia acquisition in 9M-2025 was one-off and is excluded [S3].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Negligible: non-controlling interests were Rp51.6m of equity at 30 Sep 2026 and Rp7,570k of the 9M-2026 profit, i.e. under 0.01% [S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS of Rp58.65 on EPS of Rp85.48 is a 68.6% payout [S0, S8], and the company has paid an interim every year since listing plus a final (Rp20 interim declared 1 Oct 2026, paid 13 Oct 2026, Rp258.93bn) [S7]. No dividend policy is disclosed in the filings we archived, so the payout is anchored on the last actual 68.6% rather than a house haircut; the 9M-2026 Rp496.9bn of dividends were paid from FY2025 profit and the balance sheet still carried Rp514.6bn of cash at 30 Sep 2026 [S3].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 12,946,530,200 shares in issue and no rights issue, buyback or convertibles outstanding [S3].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5% nominal: the macro deck long-run IDR inflation, with CPO prices and cash costs escalating together so real FCFF is flat after the explicit years [S0].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 selling and distribution of Rp169.4bn plus general and administrative of Rp288.5bn is 10.5% of revenue [S3]; FY2025 was 11.6% [S0]. Set at 10.5% and held flat.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies 7.30x to FY2025A EBITDA of Rp1,767.95bn (model valuation.methods.ev_ebitda.metric = 1767.954), giving Rp977.8, but section 4 says the multiple is applied 'on our FY2026E EBITDA'. On the stated FY2026E EBITDA of Rp1,999.26bn the cross-check is Rp1,108 (+13.3%), lifting the 60/25/15 blend to ~Rp1,146 and the base case to ~Rp1,221.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states that the multiple leg capitalises the last reported FY2025A EBITDA and that on FY2026E the same multiple would give a cross-check roughly an eighth higher; the prose named the wrong year, the engine metric is unchanged.

challenges.challenge: The summary says 'a move of a tenth in the deck moves the DCF by roughly a tenth of the enterprise value'; the model's own sensitivity grid gives target Rp750 at CPO x0.9 (-23%) and Rp528 at x0.8 (-46%) against Rp972 at x1.0. The stated sensitivity understates the price exposure by 2.3-4.6x, which is the single most important risk in a +107% rating.
challenges.answer: Removed the one-for-one claim. Section 4 and the summary now describe the grid: at nine-tenths of the deck the value falls about a quarter, at eight-tenths it is nearly halved, and at eleven-tenths it rises about a quarter; exact values are in the sensitivity table.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the 7.30x multiple is 'below where the large listed planters trade'. The model's own peer set has AALI 3.20x and DSNG 5.21x, and a peer median of ~6.1x (7.297 = average of peer median and the own 4-observation mean of 8.499); 7.3x is above, not below, the peer median, and the DCF implies 8.4x.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now says the 7.3x sits above the roughly 6.1x peer median (AALI a little over 3, DSNG about 5), and explains the DCF implied multiple of about 8x as an output of a deck below spot discounted at the stated WACC, not a peak-price capitalisation; the blend discounts the multiple leg by 24.5%.

challenges.challenge: The cost of equity is not reproducible from the stated inputs: rf 7.45% + 0.872 x (ERP 4.23% + CRP 2.46%) = 13.3%, not 11.66%. The engine also subtracts a -1.62% default spread (fund record:572: coe = rf - spread + beta_l*(erp_m+crp)), which section 4 omits. A reader applying the stated 13.3% would cut the DCF by ~15-18%.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now shows the full build: risk-free less the 1.62pp sovereign default spread, plus levered beta of 0.872 times ERP plus CRP, giving a COE of 11.66%, and states that a conventional build would be about two points higher.

challenges.challenge: The bear scenario shocks only CPO x0.8 and volume x0.95; it does not shock the realisation ratio, which sections 2 and 5 call the second-largest value driver and say 'if it widened further, value would fall'. A 0.75 to 0.65 realisation is a ~13% revenue cut with an EBITDA effect of the same order as the CPO shock; combined, the bear value is well below Rp553, which is still +8% above the Rp510 price.
challenges.answer: The bear case now adds a realisation shock of minus 0.10 to 0.65, sourced to the 9M2026 tape [S9], plus a one-fifth capex bulge; bear value falls to Rp363, about a third below the price. Probability stays 25% because the wedge is already in the base case.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 says a reversion of the realised ratio to the audited 0.85 'would rise' value, but the bull case shocks only CPO x1.2 and volume x1.05. On the model's own structure a 0.75 to 0.85 realisation adds ~Rp600bn of FY2027 revenue (~Rp500bn EBITDA), a larger upside than the CPO x1.2 shock and fully sourced (S8 audited 0.85).
challenges.answer: The bull case now mirrors the realisation shock at plus 0.10 to the audited 0.85 [S8] and a capex undershoot; bull value is Rp1,889. The probability set is unchanged at 25/50/25.

challenges.challenge: The model's own params_basis says the palms average 16.2 years of a 25-year bearer life [S9], and the 10-year DCF plus a 45%-of-EV Gordon terminal assumes 383 kt in perpetuity on Rp1.2m/t sustaining capex. Neither the base case, the bear case nor the risks section models the replanting trough or the capex bulge when the estate crosses its bearer life.
challenges.answer: The bear case now carries the replanting trough in volume and the capex bulge. Section 5 explains the 16.2-year average age against a 25-year bearer life [S9], why 383 kt is the matured sustainable yield rather than the peak, and that Rp1.2m/t is the actual run-rate [S3].

challenges.challenge: The method card's output contract requires a dividend-capacity yield vs NAV anchor statement; the report never states the FY2026E DPS of Rp57.93 (payout 60%) or the ~11.4% yield at Rp510, against 0.3x net debt/EBITDA and 3.4x EV/EBITDA. The dividend anchor is the one the market actually uses for IDX planters and is omitted in both directions.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states FY2026E DPS, the 68.6% payout, the resulting 13.0% yield at the current price, FCFE cover against dividends, 0.3x net debt to EBITDA and 3.4x EV/EBITDA, and names the dividend as the anchor the market is using.

challenges.challenge: Payout is set at 60% against the FY2025 actual of 68.6% (DPS 58.65 / EPS 85.48) with only 'headroom' as the basis; no company policy is cited. The base case also holds realisation at 0.75 (vs 0.85 audited), nwc at 4.5% (vs 4.1%) and cost of debt at 5.5% (vs 5.1%) - four conservative biases stacked on the drivers that set value.
challenges.answer: Payout is now the FY2025 actual 68.6% because no policy is disclosed [S0, S8]; the stacked conservatisms (realisation 0.75, working capital 4.5%, cost of debt 5.5%) are named with sources in qc_justifications.

challenges.challenge: Related-party gravity is assessed only on sales ('limited to palm kernel, no CPO'). S3 note 19 shows related-party trade payables of Rp107.8bn at 30 Sep 2026, up from Rp58.2bn (4.18% of consolidated liabilities), including PT Abadi Gemilang Investama Rp51.8bn. Purchases from affiliates are a value-destruction channel the earnings-quality screen requires quantified.
challenges.answer: Added note 19 facts F39 to F43: related-party trade payables Rp107.8bn from Rp58.2bn, 4.18% of consolidated liabilities, AGI Rp51.8bn, and related-party receivables Rp305.9bn. Sections 1, 3 and 6 quantify them, as about three per cent of cost of revenue and five per cent of assets, and classify them optics-class.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says the Rp497bn paid in 9M2026 was 'the FY2025 final and the FY2026 interim'. S3 shows the Rp496.9bn cash dividend was paid 'dari laba tahun 2025' (from FY2025 profit), while the Rp258.93bn FY2026 interim was declared 1 Oct 2026 and paid 13 Oct 2026, after the 30 Sep balance sheet. The bridge leaves that Rp259bn in 30 Sep cash and calls it 'not an adjustment', so net debt is understated by ~Rp20/share.
challenges.answer: Corrected: the Rp496.9bn paid in 9M2026 is the FY2025 final paid from FY2025 profit; the Rp258.93bn FY2026 interim was declared 1 Oct and paid 13 Oct, after the balance sheet, and is now deducted in the valuation bridge at about Rp20 per share.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says FY2026E 'EBITDA margin is below the FY2025 reported level'. FY2026E EBITDA margin is 32.72% (1,999.26/6,109.41) against FY2025 32.61% (1,767.95/5,421.39) - slightly above, not below. The same paragraph attributes it to a FY2025 biological-asset gain; S3 shows a Rp37.7bn fair-value gain in 9M2026 as well, so the explanation does not fit.
challenges.answer: Corrected: FY2026E EBITDA margin of 32.7% edges above the FY2025 32.6% rather than below it, and section 3 now cites the Rp37.7bn non-cash biological fair-value gain in 9M2026 (fact F42) and the smaller prior-year comparator [S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 pairs FY2025A debt of Rp841.6bn with cash of Rp515bn labelled 'at the last year end' and prints net debt at 0.3x. Rp515bn (F32) is the 30-Sep-2026 balance; 31-Dec-2025 cash was Rp334.4bn (S3 note 4, model FY2025A cash 334.386), and only that pairing gives net debt Rp507.2bn and 0.3x. On the printed numbers net debt is Rp326.6bn, about 0.18x, so the sentence contradicts itself.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the balance-sheet sentence: FY2025A debt of Rp841.6bn is now paired with the 31-Dec-2025 cash of Rp334.4bn (model FY2025A cash), giving net debt Rp507.2bn and the printed 0.3x, which reproduces; the 30-Sep-2026 cash of Rp515bn is stated separately as F32 and no longer paired with year-end debt [S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 states terminal growth of 2% twice ('nominal growth of 2%', 'terminal growth of 2% that is nominal only'). The model input terminal_growth is 0.025 and the assumption basis is 2.5%; the placeholder val.g with the pct0 filter renders 0.025 as 2%. A reader reproducing the DCF cannot match the printed growth to the model.
challenges.answer: Both terminal-growth placeholders now use the one-decimal filter, so section 4 prints the 2.5% terminal_growth input instead of the rounded 2%; the assumption basis already said 2.5% and no model input changed [S0].

challenges.challenge: The WACC build in section 4 uses a 9.4% pre-tax cost of debt (engine rf 7.45% plus 2.0% corporate spread) while the interest-expense forecast uses cost_of_debt 5.5%, against Rp44.8bn of FY2025 finance expense on Rp841.6bn of debt (5.3%) and Rp29.1bn in 9M2026 (5.1%). The two are never reconciled, so the disclosed WACC is not reproducible from the financing the accounts show.
challenges.answer: Added a reconciliation paragraph: the 9.4% WACC cost of debt is a market refinancing convention (risk-free plus corporate spread); the forecast and the accounts run near the 5.5% assumption, i.e. FY2025 finance expense on year-end debt and the 9M2026 finance expense, both nearer five per cent. The text states the effect at the 10.3% debt weight (about a third of a point of WACC, a few per cent of DCF) and why the market rate is retained [S3].

challenges.challenge: The P/BV leg prints Rp607 at 1.95x but anchors the book value to FY2025A equity of Rp3,644.9bn (31-Dec-2025); 3,644.9 x 1.95 / 12,946.5 = Rp550. The engine metric is Rp4,023.2bn (30-Sep-2026 equity, model valuation.methods.pbv.metric), which is what gives Rp607. The same leg also applies 1.95x to 30-Sep book without deducting the Rp258.9bn interim dividend declared 1 Oct and paid 13 Oct, which would give about Rp568; section 3 and the bridge already treat that dividend as distributed.
challenges.answer: The P/BV paragraph now quotes the 30-Sep-2026 equity attributable to owners of Rp4,023.2bn over 12,947m shares (new fact F46, Q3-2026 LK page 7), not the FY2025 year-end Rp3,644.9bn, so 4,023.2 x 1.95 / 12,947 reproduces Rp607; it also states the metric is pre the Rp258.9bn interim dividend and without the net-debt bridge, and that applying the bridge consistently would take the leg lower, not higher [S3].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg applies 7.30x to FY2025A EBITDA of Rp1,768.0bn, which contains the Cipta Davia bargain-purchase gain (Rp139.4bn in 9M2025 per S3 note 1; the note shows Rp172.5bn) plus other operating income. On underlying FY2025 EBITDA of about Rp1,579-1,629bn the leg is roughly a tenth lower, about Rp860-918 rather than Rp958. Section 4 presents the leg as a 'sanity check' without saying that its base includes a one-off the rest of the model excludes (other_nonop is zero for exactly this reason).
challenges.answer: The EV/EBITDA leg now states that its FY2025A base of Rp1,768.0bn contains the Rp172.5bn Cipta Davia bargain-purchase gain (new fact F45, LK note 1), which the forecast excludes through zero other non-operating income, so on underlying EBITDA the same multiple gives roughly nine-tenths of the printed cross-check [S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says the forecast 'is not a margin-expansion year' and that the EBITDA margin 'edges up from 32.6% in FY2025 rather than widening'. That 32.6% includes the Rp139.4bn acquisition gain, so underlying FY2025 margin is about 29-30%, and FY2026E at 32.7% is roughly 2.7-3.6pp of expansion. The paragraph explains the FY2026 margin with the 9M2026 biological gain (F42, Rp37.7bn), which does not address the FY2025 one-off in the comparison base.
challenges.answer: Dropped the no-expansion claim. Section 3 now bridges on a like-for-like base: the reported 32.6% contains the Rp172.5bn acquisition gain, so underlying FY2025 was nearer three-tenths, against which FY2026E 32.7% is real expansion driven by SG&A falling to 10.5% of revenue, a higher realised CPO price with costs held in real terms, and the Rp37.7bn biological gain, with the stronger deck rupiah a headwind [S3, S9].

missing_bull_case.note: Realisation reversion to the audited 0.85 (S8) and the ~11.4% FY2026E dividend yield are named as upside but excluded from the bull case; the dividend-capacity anchor required by the method card is absent.

missing_bear_case.note: Bear shocks only CPO x0.8 and volume x0.95; the second driver (realisation, 0.75) and the replanting/age cliff (16.2 of 25 years, params_basis) are unmodelled, and the bear value Rp553 is still above the Rp510 price.

What today price implies is the reverse DCF: at the current price the market is capitalising our own cash flows at a materially higher discount rate, or a CPO path well above the deck, and a 7.5% free float with Rp0.8bn of daily turnover is the most likely reason.
